intro.text: PART 2 — From Convex Conjugates to Variational Optimization

This continuation follows the remaining Week 1 chapter: expectations from samples, convex conjugates, optimization over functions, and the variational representation of f-divergence. Additional calculations are worked teaching examples, not additional syllabus topics.

sections.title: Why we use expectations instead of unknown density formulas

blocks.text: The chapter assumes that we can draw samples from the real-data distribution P_X and from the generator-induced distribution P_θ, even if neither density can be evaluated. For any integrable function h, E_P[h(X)] = ∫ h(x)p(x) dx. This is an exact mathematical identity. A finite-sample average is an estimate, not generally an equality.

blocks.caption: Figure 28. Integral as expectation.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Why we use expectations instead of unknown density formulas

blocks.caption: Figure 27. Expectation as weighted average.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Why we use expectations instead of unknown density formulas

blocks.text: Given independent identically distributed X₁,…,Xₙ drawn from P, the empirical estimate is (1/n) Σᵢ h(Xᵢ). Under the Law of Large Numbers assumptions (in particular, a finite expectation), it converges to E_P[h(X)] as n grows. Individual estimates fluctuate.

blocks.caption: Figure 29. Law of Large Numbers.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Why we use expectations instead of unknown density formulas

blocks.text: Worked example — estimate an unknown mean

blocks.caption: Figure 30. Monte Carlo sample average.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Why we use expectations instead of unknown density formulas

blocks.text: Observed samples: 2, 4, 3, 5, 6.
Compute the sample average: (2+4+3+5+6)/5 = 4.
Interpretation: 4 estimates the population mean. We cannot conclude that the population mean is exactly 4.

sections.title: Supremum and infimum: the language of optimization

blocks.caption: Figure 31. Maximum versus supremum.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Supremum and infimum: the language of optimization

blocks.text: A maximum must be achieved by an element of the set. A supremum is the least upper bound and need not be achieved. Likewise, a minimum is attained; an infimum need not be.
Worked example — attained versus unattained
For A=[0,1], max A=1 and sup A=1 because 1 belongs to A.
For B=(0,1), sup B=1, but max B does not exist because 1 is excluded.

blocks.caption: Figure 32. Minimum versus infimum.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Supremum and infimum: the language of optimization

blocks.text: For C=(2,5), inf C=2, but min C does not exist because 2 is excluded.

sections.title: Convex conjugates: definition, optimization and geometry

blocks.caption: Figure 33. Quadratic conjugate optimization.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Convex conjugates: definition, optimization and geometry

blocks.text: For a function f, its convex conjugate is f*(t) = supᵤ {t u − f(u)}, with the supremum taken over the domain of f. We fix t, vary u, and take the largest possible objective value. The conjugate is a new function of t. It is convex, even when f is not convex.
Worked example — conjugate of a quadratic

blocks.caption: Figure 35. Quadratic conjugate solution.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Convex conjugates: definition, optimization and geometry

blocks.text: Start with f(u)=u²/2 for all real u. Then f*(t)=supᵤ (t u−u²/2).
Differentiate with respect to u: d/du(tu−u²/2)=t−u. The stationary point is u=t.
The second derivative is −1, so this is the unique maximum.
Substitute u=t: f*(t)=t²−t²/2=t²/2.
For t=2, the maximizing input is u=2 and the maximum value is f*(2)=2.
Geometric interpretation: for convex differentiable f, a supporting line of slope t has the form y=t u−f*(t) when the supremum is attained. Its vertical intercept is −f*(t).

blocks.caption: Figure 34. Supporting tangent geometry.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Convex conjugates: definition, optimization and geometry

blocks.text: Worked example — the conjugate used for KL divergence

blocks.caption: Figure 36. KL convex conjugate.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Convex conjugates: definition, optimization and geometry

blocks.text: Use f(u)=u ln u for u>0, extended continuously by f(0)=0; the optimization domain is u≥0.
Form t u−u ln u. Its derivative for u>0 is t−(ln u+1).
Set it to zero: ln u=t−1, hence u=e^(t−1).
The objective is strictly concave on u>0 (second derivative −1/u).
Substitution gives f*(t)=e^(t−1).
Note the distinction between f(u)=u ln u, used in the KL f-divergence, and f*(t)=e^(t−1), its convex conjugate. They are different functions.

blocks.caption: Figure 37. Biconjugate identity.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Why the biconjugate representation matters

blocks.text: For a proper, convex, lower-semicontinuous function f, the biconjugate identity is f(u)=supₜ {t u−f*(t)}. This converts an expression involving f into an optimization over a scalar t. The conditions matter: the identity is not valid without qualification for every arbitrary function.
Worked example — recover the quadratic
Take f*(t)=t²/2.
For a fixed u, maximize t u−t²/2 over t.
Derivative with respect to t is u−t, so t=u.
The maximum is u²−u²/2=u²/2=f(u).

sections.title: Why the optimizing scalar becomes a function T(x)

blocks.caption: Figure 38. A scalar-valued function T.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Why the optimizing scalar becomes a function T(x)

blocks.text: In f-divergence the density ratio p(x)/q(x) depends on the location x. Therefore the optimizing scalar t can also depend on x. Write t=T(x), where T maps the data space X to the real numbers. T(x₁), T(x₂), and T(x₃) may be different, but they need not be.

The optimization variable is now an entire function T, not one fixed number. A function class 𝒯 is a collection of candidate functions. Restricting this class may make optimization more practical, but the supremum over a restricted class cannot exceed that over the full admissible class.

blocks.caption: Figure 40. Function class.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Why the optimizing scalar becomes a function T(x)

blocks.caption: Figure 39. Pointwise and function optimization.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Why the optimizing scalar becomes a function T(x)

blocks.caption: Figure 43. Variational objective.
blocks.alt: Illustration: The variational representation of f-divergence

blocks.text: Let P be the real distribution and Q the model distribution. Under the standard regularity and admissibility assumptions, the variational f-divergence representation is D_f(P∥Q) = sup_T { E_P[T(X)] − E_Q[f*(T(X))] }. Here f is the generating convex function with f(1)=0, and f* is its convex conjugate.
The first expectation is taken over real samples P. The second is taken over generated samples Q. Crucially, the SAME T appears in both terms, and f* acts on T(X) only in the second expectation.

blocks.caption: Figure 42. Real and generated samples.
blocks.alt: Illustration: The variational representation of f-divergence

blocks.text: How the formula arises: starting from D_f(P∥Q)=∫q(x)f(p(x)/q(x))dx, replace f(r) by supₜ {tr−f*(t)}. For each x the ratio r=p(x)/q(x) can select a value T(x). Under appropriate conditions permitting the supremum to be exchanged with integration, this yields sup_T ∫[p(x)T(x)−q(x)f*(T(x))]dx, equal to the displayed difference of expectations.
A restriction to 𝒯 gives sup_{T∈𝒯} J(T) ≤ D_f(P∥Q), where J(T)=E_P[T]−E_Q[f*(T)], provided 𝒯 is contained in the admissible function class. Equality is possible if 𝒯 is sufficiently expressive.

blocks.caption: Figure 41. Restricted function class.
blocks.alt: Illustration: The variational representation of f-divergence

blocks.text: Worked example — variational objective for KL
For f(u)=u ln u, the conjugate is f*(t)=e^(t−1).
Substitute into the general representation: KL(P∥Q)=sup_T { E_P[T(X)]−E_Q[e^(T(X)−1)] }.
The inner optimization searches for a suitable scalar-valued function T.
With a restricted function family, maximizing the same expression yields a lower bound, not automatically the exact KL divergence.

blocks.caption: Figure 44. Empirical sample-average objective.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Turning expectations into empirical objectives

blocks.text: For observed real samples x₁,…,xₙ and generated samples x̃₁,…,x̃ₘ, estimate J(T) by Ĵ(T)=(1/n)ΣᵢT(xᵢ)−(1/m)Σⱼf*(T(x̃ⱼ)). This is an empirical objective. For a fixed integrable T, sample averages approximate their corresponding expectations. Optimizing the empirical supremum introduces additional statistical considerations; do not assume the optimized estimate is automatically unbiased.
Worked example — evaluate a fixed empirical objective
Suppose the two real sample values of T are 1 and 3, giving average (1+3)/2=2.
Suppose the two generated sample values of f*(T) are 0.8 and 1.2, giving average (0.8+1.2)/2=1.
Then the empirical objective at this fixed T is Ĵ(T)=2−1=1.
This is not automatically the supremum and is not automatically the true divergence.

Real samples reveal the data distribution indirectly. A generator turns random latent inputs into model samples. We want the model distribution to approach the real one, and f-divergences give mathematical comparisons. Convexity and convex conjugates transform divergence expressions into optimizations over functions, whose expectations can be estimated from samples.
Question 1 — What is the difference between maximum and supremum?
A maximum must belong to the set. A supremum is the least upper bound and may lie outside it.
Question 2 — What is f*(t) for f(u)=u²/2?
f*(t)=t²/2; the maximizing u equals t.
Question 3 — What is f*(t) for f(u)=u ln u?
f*(t)=e^(t−1), with u≥0 and natural logarithms.
Question 4 — Why introduce T(x)?
The density ratio depends on x, so the maximizing scalar can depend on x; a function represents these pointwise choices.
Question 5 — Which expectation uses generated samples?
The second term E_{P_θ}[f*(T(X))].
Question 6 — Why does restricting 𝒯 produce a lower bound?
A supremum over a subset cannot exceed the supremum over the full admissible set.
